query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid, transient heating that synchronizes nucleation across all noble metal precursors is the key mechanistic driver for forming homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles. In contrast, slower heating permits differential nucleation and elemental diffusion, leading to phase separation and heterogeneous structures.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneously mixed multimetal precursor system containing noble metal ions or complexes (often with similar ligand environments) that have not yet been reduced or nucleated.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid, high-temperature thermal shock (or equivalent transient heating process) versus a conventional slower heating method while maintaining all other synthesis parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Under inert or reducing atmosphere with controlled temperature ramp rates, where a very high heating rate (milliseconds to seconds scale) is used to induce nearly simultaneous nucleation.
generation.structural_mediator: The brief but intense thermal pulse mediates simultaneous reduction and nucleation of all metal species, minimizing time for elemental segregation and enabling full solid-solution alloying at the nanoscale.
generation.mechanism: A high transient temperature minimizes differences in individual nucleation activation energies among the noble metals, forcing them to nucleate nearly concurrently. The rapid quenching that follows locks in the homogeneous alloy structure while preserving high surface atom exposure needed for catalysis.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized using rapid transient heating will exhibit a single, homogeneous solid-solution phase with uniform elemental distribution and high noble metal surface exposure. In contrast, slower heating will lead to phase-separated domains, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized under a conventional, slower heating regime that allows element-specific nucleation and diffusion, resulting in heterogeneous phase formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply to systems with moderate differences in metal reduction or nucleation energies (typically up to five or seven elements) and when precursor ligand environments do not overly bias individual metal kinetics. It may not hold in cases with extreme disparities in metal chemistry or when additional factors (e.g., solvent or stabilizer effects) dominate the nucleation process.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal heating rate and pulse duration needed to achieve complete simultaneous nucleation remain to be precisely determined. Additionally, the role of precursor chemistry and ligand stripping during reactive heating introduces uncertainty that may require further tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles from an identical multimetal precursor mix under two thermal regimes: one with rapid transient heating (e.g. using a carbothermal shock setup) and one with a standard slower heating protocol. Use otherwise identical reaction conditions (atmosphere, precursor concentration, solvent, etc.).
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess elemental homogeneity.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis to determine phase purity and crystallinity.
Surface area and catalytic activity measurements to evaluate the exposure of noble metal active sites.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the transient heating condition does not yield significantly more homogeneous, single-phase nanoparticles with enhanced noble metal surface exposure compared to the slower heating condition, then the hypothesis that synchronized nucleation via rapid heating governs successful HEA nanoparticle formation would be falsified.

Unveiling Fundamentals of Multi-Beam Pulsed Laser Ablation in Liquids toward Scaling up Nanoparticle Production

Abstract: AbstractPulsed laser ablation in liquids (PLAL) is a versatile technique to produce high-purity colloidal nanoparticles. Despite considerable recent progress in increasing the productivity of the technique, there is still significant demand for a practical, cost-effective method for upscaling PLAL synthesis. Here we employ and unveil the fundamentals of multi-beam (MB) PLAL. The MB-PLAL upscaling approach can bypass the cavitation bubble, the main limiting factor of PLAL efficiency, by splitting the laser beam into several beams using static diffractive optical elements (DOEs). A multimetallic high-entropy alloy CrFeCoNiMn was used as a model material and the productivity of its nanoparticles in the MB-PLAL setup was investigated and compared with that in the standard single-beam PLAL. General negative pressure annealing approach for creating ultra-high-loading single atom catalyst libraries

Abstract: AbstractCatalyst systems populated by high-density single atoms are crucial for improving catalytic activity and selectivity, which can potentially maximize the industrial prospects of heterogeneous single-atom catalysts (SACs). However, achieving high-loading SACs with metal contents above 10 wt% remains challenging. Here we describe a general negative pressure annealing strategy to fabricate ultrahigh-loading SACs with metal contents up to 27.3–44.8 wt% for 13 different metals on a typical carbon nitride matrix. Furthermore, our approach enables the synthesis of high-entropy single-atom catalysts (HESACs) that exhibit the coexistence of multiple metal single atoms with high metal contents. In-situ aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM (AC-STEM) combined with ex-situ X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) demonstrate that the negative pressure annealing treatment accelerates the removal of anionic ligand in metal precursors and boosts the bonding of metal species with N defective sites, enabling the formation of dense N-coordinated metal sites. Electronic descriptors for designing high-entropy alloy electrocatalysts by leveraging local chemical environments

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a vast compositional space for fine-tuning electrocatalytic activities, leveraging millions of distinct active sites on the surface. However, the intricate local chemical environment poses challenges to the rational and efficient design of HEA electrocatalysts with high reactivity. Here, focusing on noble-metal HEAs for oxygen reduction reactions, we propose a straightforward yet effective descriptor for quantitively determining the local reactivities of HEAs. This descriptor is based on a linear combination of the intrinsic d-band filling of the active center and the neighborhood electronegativity. Our model offers an accurate and robust description of the binding strengths of intermediates with different adsorption configurations on HEAs, supported by external density functional theory calculations. Importantly, the local environmental electronegativity of the HEA surface is strongly related to the d-band profile of the center atom(s) embedded within. Highly efficient decomposition of ammonia using high-entropy alloy catalysts

Abstract: Ammonia represents a promising liquid fuel for hydrogen storage, but its large-scale application is limited by the need for precious metal ruthenium (Ru) as catalyst. Here we report on highly efficient ammonia decomposition using novel high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalysts made of earth abundant elements. Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram. These HEA nanoparticles demonstrate substantially enhanced catalytic activity and stability for ammonia decomposition, with improvement factors achieving >20 versus Ru catalysts. Catalytic activity of HEA nanoparticles is robustly tunable by varying the Co/Mo ratio, allowing for the optimization of surface property to maximize the reactivity under different reaction conditions.
